content: # Variable Interpolation in Echo Strings vs. Output Escaping The core issue isn't that you can't add a variable to an `echo` statement; it is how PHP handles string parsing relative to HTML tags. In your specific example: ```php $link_address = '#'; echo '<a href="$link_address">Link</a>'; ``` You are explicitly outputting the HTML entities (`<`, `>`, `"`) rather than the raw characters `<`, `>`, and `"`. When PHP processes this line, it prints the literal text `<a href="$link_address">Link</a>` to the browser. The browser then renders that text exactly as written, treating `$link_address` as plain text inside a string, not as a variable to be resolved. To make this work, you need to switch from outputting escaped HTML entities to outputting raw characters so PHP can interpolate the variable. However, mixing raw variables directly into HTML strings without care often leads to security vulnerabilities or broken markup if the variable contains unexpected data. ## Using Double Quotes for Interpolation The most straightforward solution is to ensure your echo string uses double quotes instead of single quotes and avoids manual HTML entity escaping. PHP evaluates variables inside double-quoted strings automatically. ```php $link_address = '/about'; echo "Link"; ``` In this scenario, PHP outputs: `Link`. The browser receives the raw HTML string and correctly renders the link. This approach is standard for simple cases where you are generating static or semi-dynamic content. It relies on the assumption that the variable `$link_address` contains a valid URL without malicious script tags that could execute within your own context. ## Security Considerations with User Input The critical trade-off appears when `$link_address` comes from user input rather than server-side logic. If you allow users to define their own links, simply echoing them into the `href` attribute can lead to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities. An attacker could inject a payload like `javascript:alert(1)` or an SVG injection attack if they control the URL. To handle this safely, you must sanitize the input before embedding it in the HTML string.
